segments.text: Welcome to your daily Robotics news digest for October 16, 2026.
Today we cover Pudu's expansion, Tesla's new skin tech, and AI learning physical skills.
Tune in for the latest.
From Robotics & Automation News, Pudu expands beyond service robots into semi-humanoids and quadrupeds.
This report details the company's development of advanced robotic platforms including semi-humanoids and quadrupeds showcased at the IFA 2026 exhibition.
At the event, Pudu displayed the industrial semi-humanoid D7 and the quadruped D5-W robot.
The D7 features its primary joint concentration in the arms, waist, and head, presenting a design alternative for industrial applications.
The D5-W robot integrates both wheeled and legged locomotion, enabling navigation over uneven terrain and autonomous recovery from falls.
Furthermore, Pudu is enhancing the autonomy of its current commercial robotics, demonstrated by the self-evaluating cleaning robot.
This development signals a shift in robotic design toward more complex, versatile physical forms.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Tesla patent reveals touch-sensitive skin for robot hands".
This report details a US patent filed by Tesla for a touch-sensitive skin designed for robot hands, which allows for the detection of contact, force, and pressure.
The technology involves printing tactile sensors onto flexible materials and subsequently heat-forming them into three-dimensional shapes.
These sensors operate by utilizing overlapping conductive regions on flexible substrates to detect pressure changes through capacitive and piezoresistive methods.
The patent further emphasizes manufacturability through techniques such as screen printing and thermoforming to facilitate scalable production of this material.
This innovation seeks to enhance humanoid robots' dexterity by providing them with sensory feedback regarding object manipulation.
The development indicates a progression toward more sophisticated tactile sensing in robotic systems.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Skild AI trains robots to learn physical skills through self-play".
This report details a self-play training method developed by Skild AI that enables robots to acquire physical skills without requiring human demonstrations.
The key finding is that robots autonomously learned complex physical behaviors, such as soccer skills, by playing against increasingly capable versions of themselves within a simulated environment.
This process allowed the robots to develop intricate physical actions like dribbling and tackling based solely on the objective of scoring.
The learned policy was subsequently successfully transferred to a physical humanoid robot, indicating potential for physical artificial general intelligence.
This methodology seeks to decrease the dependence on human demonstration data for teaching robots complex physical tasks.
The development suggests a pathway toward more autonomous physical skill acquisition in robotics.
From Robotics & Automation News, ETH Zurich scientists turn WUJI robotic hand into self-propelled mobile manipulator.
This report details the transformation of a WUJI robotic hand into a self-propelled mobile manipulator capable of independent locomotion.

The research achieved this by enabling the hand to crawl, recover from falls, and move autonomously using its fingers for propulsion, functioning as a compact mobile manipulator without an external mobility mechanism.
Reinforcement learning was the methodology employed to develop these locomotion skills by considering the unique characteristics of each finger.
The system demonstrates that the manipulator itself can execute both locomotion and manipulation functions simultaneously.
This work indicates progress toward integrated, self-sufficient robotic systems in the field of artificial intelligence and robotics.
From Robohub, "Robot Talk Episode 166 – Evolving robot bodies and brains, with Rika Antonova"

reports on the use of artificial intelligence to develop complementary robot hardware and algorithms with Rika Antonova from the University of Cambridge, highlighting advancements in co-design and automated algorithm discovery in robotics.
Claire discussed this collaboration, focusing on the evolving development of robot bodies and brains.

The research involved exploring the integration of artificial intelligence to create complementary systems for robot hardware and algorithms, drawing upon Rika Antonova's expertise in co-design, automated algorithm discovery, and data-efficient reinforcement learning in robotics, building upon her background from Stanford University.
The work details the methodology employed in developing these integrated systems, focusing on efficient learning processes for autonomous machine development.
This work suggests a trajectory toward more integrated and intelligently designed robotic systems in the near future.
From Humanoid.guide, "PNDbotics Adam humanoid climbs 1 meter box, post claims".
This report details an achievement by the PNDbotics Adam humanoid demonstrating the ability to ascend a one-meter high box.
The movement involved analyzing the obstacle, planning movements, and executing a sequence where one foot was placed on top before weight transfer.
This climb necessitated coordinated movement across the robot's body to support and elevate itself while maintaining equilibrium.
The sequence highlighted the preceding analysis of the obstacle and the planning of the movements before actual foot placement occurred.
This capability was communicated via a post on LinkedIn by Space and Technology.
The demonstration indicates advancements in real-world problem-solving for advanced artificial intelligence systems.
Further testing of such locomotion skills is anticipated in the robotics sector.
From Waymo Blog, "Hello Toronto! Waymo is En Route".
This report details Waymo's plan to launch its fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto, aiming for first riders in 2028 through investment in local infrastructure and employment.
The rollout will commence with a phased, safety-first approach utilizing high-definition mapping and testing with autonomous specialists operating within Toronto's driving conditions.
This expansion includes a partnership with Element Fleet Management for end-to-end fleet management and job creation opportunities.
Data from over four hundred million autonomous kilometers indicates that autonomous vehicles have demonstrated significantly lower crash rates compared to human drivers.
The service also incorporates collaborations with mobility advocacy organizations to prioritize safety and accessibility.
This progression signals continued development in autonomous transportation technology and its integration into urban environments.
From Planet ROS, "ROS Discourse General: Logging and Observability Guide Review Part 4 | Cloud Robotics WG Meeting 2026-10-19"
reports on the proceedings of a Cloud Robotics Working Group meeting focused on refining a key documentation.
The group convened on Monday, October 19, 2026, with scheduled sessions at four PM and five PM UTC.
During the meeting, the group proceeded with the editing of the first draft of the Logging and Observability guide.
The objective of this session was to finalize the guide and prepare it for distribution to guest speakers for subsequent review.
Information regarding the meeting link and notifications is available through designated channels for attendance.
This work represents a step in standardizing logging and observability practices within the cloud robotics domain.
Future updates will follow the distribution of the revised guide.

From thesequence.substack.com, The Sequence Robotics - Issue 952: One Brain, Many Bodies: Inside Skild AI's Robotics Bet details Skild AI's research into transferring robotic intelligence across different hardware.
This research focuses on motor adaptation, video-prompted task learning, and self-play to achieve this intelligence transferability.
The core concept involves separating intelligence from the physical machine, testing whether these capabilities can withstand real-world requirements for speed, reliability, and safety in deployment.
The methodology involves training models to learn how to understand a body rather than requiring explicit specification of every physical detail upfront.
The company is testing the viability of this approach by pushing the learned skills into physical systems.
This development suggests a shift toward more adaptable and generalized artificial intelligence systems in robotics.
And that's all the circuits for today!
Hope your day is as smoothly programmed as a perfectly executed algorithm.
Keep building, and we'll see you tomorrow.
